On 20 September 1924 John Marshall, head of the Archaeological Survey of India, announced in a London magazine that a forgotten civilisation had been found in the Indus valley. It pushed the start of Indian history back by more than two thousand years.

Until then the story began with the Vedas and, in stone, with Ashoka. The mounds at Harappa in Punjab were known, and in the 1850s railway builders had carted away their bricks to lay track. An odd seal from the site was published in 1875 and puzzled everyone.

In 1921 Daya Ram Sahni dug at Harappa. In 1922 R. D. Banerji, looking at a Buddhist mound 600 kilometres south in Sindh, found the same seals beneath it at Mohenjo-daro. Marshall saw that the two sites were one culture, older than anything known in India.

A week after his article a scholar wrote in to say that the same seals had turned up in Mesopotamia in levels of the third millennium BCE. That gave the date.

Large digs followed and revealed planned streets, drains and the great bath (see Mohenjo-daro and the Indus Valley civilisation). After 1947 the main sites lay in Pakistan, and Indian teams found many more in Gujarat and Haryana. The script is still unread.
